Activation-patching conclusions depend on corruption, measurement, and patch scope. Zhang and Nanda find that Gaussian noise versus semantically matched token replacement can yield different localization; probability can miss harmful components, and sliding-window patches can exaggerate localization relative to individual-layer effects. Favor realistic replacement histories and test robustness across plausible corruptions. Natural donor activations still do not guarantee that the resulting hybrid computation is in distribution. Interpret effects as conditional on the intervention, rather than proof that a component uniquely stores a behavior. [Best Practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042), [Patching Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255v1).

For recommendation, a useful adaptation is to select a negative competitor before intervention and hold its identity fixed: Δ[s(target)−s(competitor)] measures a consistent contrast. Recomputing the maximum competitor after every patch changes the compared item and can introduce switching effects; report that margin separately. Maximum-competitor margin concerns top-1 performance, whereas HR@10 depends on crossing the tenth-negative score. Continuous contrasts support exploratory localization; paired changes in target rank and HR@10 verify relevance to the actual benchmark. Keep candidate sets and tie handling fixed. These recommendation-specific practices are deductions from the metric arguments, not directly validated findings from those papers. [Metric Discussion](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255v1).

Random-circuit hypothesis tests provide stronger evidence than knockdown alone. Recommended controls: random patches matched for component count, layer, position, and intervention magnitude; identity patches; unrelated donors; and both restoration and disruption directions. Separate exploratory site selection from confirmation on unused examples, report paired uncertainty, and correct for multiple comparisons across searched sites and metrics. A large selected effect without matched controls supports a weaker localization claim. [Circuit Hypothesis Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13032).
